what_it_does: Virtual memory is the operating system's trick of giving every program the illusion that it owns a large, private address space, while the OS secretly maps those 'virtual' addresses to physical locations in RAM and on disk. Studying how virtual memory hardware and OS software interact is important for designing faster, more efficient systems, but it is very hard to do: running a real OS inside a simulator is accurate but painfully slow, while fast simulators skip the OS details and produce misleading results. Virtuoso introduces a new simulation method called 'imitation-based OS simulation': researchers first capture traces of real OS decisions — which pages to allocate, which to evict from RAM, how to manage the address-translation cache (called a TLB, or Translation Lookaside Buffer) — from a real Linux kernel running real workloads. A lightweight simulator then replays those recorded decisions with cycle-accurate hardware timing, rather than re-running the full OS logic. The result is a simulator that is fast enough for rapid experimentation but accurate enough to catch real hardware/OS interactions that coarse simulators miss.
